h1: Pool Grounding and Bonding Inspection in Broward County
intro: If someone in the family says they feel a little tingle in the pool, that is not their imagination, and it is not something to swim through and hope it goes away. On an older pool, the grounding and bonding that keeps you safe can quietly fail while everything still looks fine. Every metal part around the water, the rails, the ladder, the light housing, the fittings, is supposed to be tied into one grounding system, so that if a wire ever leaks current, the breaker trips instead of a swimmer taking the shock. A pool grounding and bonding inspection tests that connection, part by part, and proves it under load. We find the weak link before anyone feels it, and we tell you plainly what it takes to fix.

definition.heading: What a pool grounding and bonding inspection actually is
definition.body: Bonding and grounding are two jobs that work together. Bonding ties all the metal around your pool into one connected network, so everything sits at the same electrical level and there is no difference in charge for a swimmer to feel. Grounding gives fault current a safe path back, so the breaker can sense trouble and shut the circuit off. An inspection verifies both. We locate the bonding grid, check the connections at the pump, the equipment, the rails, and the lights, and we test that the whole system is continuous and doing its job. Where a connection has corroded or was never made, we show you, explain what it means, and lay out the correction. It is measured, not guessed.

symptoms.title: A tingle in the water
symptoms.body: Swimmers feel a faint buzz or tingle when they touch a rail, a ladder, or the light, and it fades when they let go. That sensation is current finding a path it should never take. It is the clearest warning sign there is.

symptoms.title: An older pool or older equipment
symptoms.body: Your pool is a few decades old, or the equipment has been swapped out over the years by different hands. Bonding connections loosen, corrode, and get left off during repairs, and no one goes back to check them.

symptoms.title: Breakers tripping on pool circuits
symptoms.body: A pump, heater, or light breaker keeps tripping for no reason you can see. The breaker is often sensing a real ground fault. It is doing its job, and it is telling you the grounding system needs a look.

symptoms.title: Recent equipment work
symptoms.body: A new pump, heater, or salt system went in, but the bonding wire was not reconnected the way it should have been. New equipment on an old bond is one of the most common ways protection quietly disappears.

symptoms.title: Corrosion you can see
symptoms.body: You notice rust or green corrosion on the bonding lug at the pump, or the wire looks broken, brittle, or disconnected. Corrosion is the enemy of a bond, and South Florida moisture and pool chemistry speed it up.

symptoms.title: It has never been tested
symptoms.body: The pool has been in the ground for years and the bonding has never been checked. Nothing looks wrong, but grounding is something you do not see, you only feel the effect, and by then someone is in the water.

process.body: You reach a licensed electrician directly, day or night. We ask what you are seeing, whether anyone has felt tingling, how old the pool is, and what equipment has changed. That phone triage tells us what to bring and how soon you need us.

process.title: We come out and test the system
process.body: We come to the property and inspect the pool electrical system in person. We locate the bonding grid, check every connection, and test continuity across the rails, ladder, lights, and equipment. Electricity is something you feel the effect of, so we measure it instead of guessing.

process.title: One honest price, based on what we find
process.body: We show you what passed and what did not, in plain language, and give you one straightforward price for the correction. We price it once and price it right, so there are no surprises after we start. If it is a quick fix, we tell you that too.

process.title: Our own crew does the work
process.body: Our in-house crew makes the corrections: reconnecting bonds, replacing corroded lugs, and re-establishing the grounding path so every metal part is tied in. We stay in our lane and do the complete job, not a patch that fails next season.

process.title: Permit, inspection, and a follow-up
process.body: When the work calls for it, we pull the permit and the building department signs it off, and we are there to meet the inspector. Once it passes, the safety question is settled on the record. Then we follow up to make sure you are comfortable.

benefits.title: Peace of mind in the water
benefits.body: You and your family swim knowing every metal part is bonded and any fault trips the breaker instead of reaching a body. That is the whole point, and you get to stop wondering.

benefits.title: A problem caught before it is felt
benefits.body: Testing finds the broken bond while the pool still looks fine, not after someone reports a shock. We would rather find it on a meter than have you find it in the water.

benefits.title: A clear, honest record
benefits.body: You get a plain explanation of what we checked and what we corrected, and when the work is permitted, the building department approval backs it up. No mystery, no jargon.

benefits.title: Work that holds up
benefits.body: Our crew does the complete correction with materials that stand up to South Florida moisture and pool chemistry, so the protection you pay for is still there years from now.

localSections.heading: Older South Florida pools and the bonding they were built with
localSections.body: A lot of South Florida pools went in during the building waves of the 1960s through the 1980s, and many of the homes from West Palm Beach down to North Miami Beach still have their original pools. The bonding standards those pools were built to were looser than what the code asks for today, and even a pool that met code back then has had decades of pumps, heaters, and lights swapped in and out. Every one of those changes is a chance for a bond to get left off. On top of that, the older the community, the more it matters, because a younger body can shrug off a shock that an older person cannot. That is why we pay close attention to pools in established neighborhoods and older communities. The equipment looks modern, but the grounding underneath it can be forty years behind.

localSections.heading: Heat, humidity, and salt air work against a bond
localSections.body: Bonding depends on solid metal-to-metal connections, and South Florida is hard on metal. Year-round humidity, salt in the air near the coast, and pool water chemistry all attack the lugs, clamps, and wire that hold a bonding system together. A connection that was tight and clean the day it was installed can be green with corrosion a decade later, and corrosion is resistance, which is exactly what a bond cannot have. Heat cycles loosen fittings over the seasons, and equipment that runs hard through our long swim season vibrates connections loose. None of this is visible from the deck. It happens slowly at the lug and inside the conduit, and the first sign is often a swimmer feeling something they should never feel. That is why the connection has to be tested, not eyeballed, and why once a year is the honest cadence here.

localSections.heading: How Broward handles pool electrical work
localSections.body: Pool electrical work is exactly the kind of job building departments across Broward County watch closely, and that is a good thing for you. Inspectors are thorough on bonding and grounding because they know what is at stake, and a permit means a second trained set of eyes confirms the work is right. When a correction needs a permit, we pull it, do the work to current code, and we meet the inspector in person to prove the grounding under test. Once it passes, the responsibility question is settled on the public record, not on somebody word. Some smaller fixes do not require a permit, and we will tell you honestly which is which. What we will not do is cut a corner to skip an inspection. The whole value of doing pool work correctly is that the building department gets to say it is correct.

localSections.heading: What this means with your insurance
localSections.body: Insurance carriers in South Florida have grown careful about anything that mixes water and electricity, and a pool is right at that intersection. Carriers increasingly want to see that a property electrical systems are safe and properly maintained, and a permitted, inspected correction gives you documentation you can point to. If a carrier or an inspector ever asks whether your pool bonding was addressed by a licensed contractor, a closed permit and a passed inspection answer the question cleanly. We do not file claims or speak for your carrier, and every policy is different, so we will not promise how yours will treat it. What we can tell you is that doing the work through the permit process leaves you with a clear paper trail instead of a verbal assurance, and that record tends to help far more than it hurts.

guide.title: The complete guide to pool grounding and bonding

sections.heading: Bonding and grounding: two jobs, one safety net
sections.body: Two words get used like they mean the same thing, and they do not: bonding and grounding. Bonding is the job of tying every piece of metal in and around your pool into one connected network. The rails, the ladder, the pump housing, the heater, the light niche, the rebar in the deck, even the water itself through a bonding fitting, all get linked so they sit at the same electrical level. When everything is at the same level, there is no difference in charge between two things a swimmer might touch at once, and with no difference, there is nothing to feel. Grounding is the separate job of giving fault current a fast, safe path back to the source so the breaker can sense it and shut off. Bonding keeps you from feeling a difference. Grounding makes sure a real fault trips the breaker. You need both, and they have to be connected to each other correctly. On a healthy pool, a wire that starts leaking current sends that fault straight back through the ground path, the breaker trips in a fraction of a second, and the swimmer never knows anything happened. On a pool where the bond is broken or the ground path has corroded through, that same leak has nowhere clean to go, so it sits on a metal rail and waits for a hand. Everything on the surface looks identical. The only way to tell the two apart is to test, and that is the whole reason an inspection exists, because guessing has no place around a pool.

sections.heading: The pool that tingles, and why the breaker never knew
sections.body: Here is how it goes wrong in the real world. On an older pool, grounding and bonding can quietly fail while the pool keeps running and looks completely normal. A wire in the pump or the light circuit starts to leak a small amount of current, which is common as insulation ages in our heat and moisture. If every metal part is properly bonded into the grounding system, that leak trips the breaker and everyone is safe, and you never even learn it happened. If the bond is broken, the story is different. The leaked current energizes the metal it can reach, a rail or a light housing or a fitting, and because the breaker cannot sense a fault that has no path back to it, the breaker never trips. It has no idea anything is wrong. Then someone touches the rail, becomes the path the current was looking for, and feels the shock. That tingle people describe in the water is the early warning, and it is a warning you should never ignore. We have answered exactly these calls. Someone in the family felt a buzz on the ladder, and the fix was to find the broken bond, restore the connection, and prove under test that a fault now trips the breaker the way it always should have. The reassuring part is that the failure is findable and fixable. The dangerous part is that nothing about it announces itself until a person completes the circuit.

sections.heading: When a bonding correction stops being optional
sections.body: Most of the time, a bonding correction is something you choose to do because you want the pool to be safe. There are moments when it stops being a choice. If anyone has felt tingling or taken a shock in or around the pool, the work needs to happen now, before the pool is used again. If a breaker on a pool circuit is tripping and the cause traces back to a ground fault, the system is telling you plainly that protection is compromised. When you replace major equipment, a pump, a heater, a light, or a salt system, code expects the bonding to be brought up to current standards as part of that work, not left the way it was. And any time an inspector, a home inspector during a sale, or a licensed electrician flags a bonding deficiency, that finding does not go away by ignoring it. The honest way to think about it is simple. A pool is one of the few places in daily life where a hidden electrical fault meets a wet human body with almost no resistance between them. That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to test once and correct what the test finds.

sections.heading: What happens the day we test your pool
sections.body: When we come out, the visit is methodical, and you are welcome to watch the whole thing. We start at the equipment pad, because that is where the bonding grid ties together and where corrosion shows up first. We check the bonding lug on the pump, the heater, and any other equipment, looking for connections that are loose, corroded, painted over, or simply never made. Then we work outward to the pool itself, testing continuity to the rails, the ladder, the light housing, and the deck bonding where the pool was built with it. Continuity is the real test. We are confirming that every metal part is electrically connected to every other, with no break and no high-resistance corroded joint pretending to be a connection. If we find a fault, we do not just tell you it failed. We show you where, explain in plain terms what that gap means for a swimmer, and walk you through what the correction involves. You will understand the problem before we ever talk about fixing it. When the testing is done, you have a clear picture: what is protecting you, what is not, and what it takes to close the gap. No pressure, no scare tactics, just what the meter says and what we recommend.

sections.heading: What it costs, and why per property is the honest answer
sections.body: People want a number over the phone, and we understand why, but the honest answer for pool bonding is that it depends on what we find. Our service call is $240, which covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis. If the problem turns out to be something we can handle on the spot during that visit, there is no separate return charge. From there, the correction is quoted per property after we have tested the system, because no two older pools have failed in the same way. One pool needs a single corroded lug replaced and re-bonded. Another has three connections that were never made and a light niche that was never tied in. Pricing the second one like the first would be a guess, and a guess is how people get overcharged or undercharged. We price it once and price it right, based on what the test actually shows, so the number you get is the number for the work you need. If deeper faults turn up that point toward a larger repair or a service rebuild, we will tell you that honestly rather than patch a system that needs more. You are paying for the experience that knows the difference.

sections.heading: How to choose someone for pool electrical work
sections.body: Pool electrical is specialized, and not every electrician takes it on, because the liability when it is done wrong is real. When you are choosing someone, a few things matter more than price. First, licensing. You want a licensed electrical contractor who works on pools regularly, not a handyman and not a pool cleaner reaching outside their trade. Ask whether they are licensed and whether they pull permits. Second, permits and inspections. The right answer to the permit question is yes, gladly, because a permit means the building department confirms the work, and on pool bonding an inspector is thorough for good reason. Anyone who wants to skip the permit to save you a little money is also skipping the proof that the work is correct. Third, whether they test rather than guess. Bonding is invisible, so a proper job is measured and proven under load, not eyeballed and declared fine. We will not run down another contractor to win your trust. We would rather earn it by explaining the work clearly, doing it completely, and letting the inspector confirm it. When someone shows you the problem on a meter, tells you plainly what it costs, and welcomes the inspection, you are in good hands.

sections.heading: Why once a year, and why before heater season
sections.body: You do not need us at the pool every month, and we will never tell you that you do. The honest cadence for a pool electrical inspection is once a year, and the best time is before heater season. In South Florida our pools run year round, and the heater comes on when the weather finally cools, which is exactly when circuits get worked hardest and when a marginal bond is most likely to show itself. Checking the bonding before you lean on the heater means you catch a weak connection in the fall instead of discovering it mid-winter with the family in the water. A yearly test is quick, it is inexpensive next to what it protects, and for an older pool it is the single most sensible piece of maintenance you are probably not doing. Newer pools built to current bonding standards are in better shape and need less worry. Older pools in older communities are where a yearly look earns its keep. That is the whole recommendation, stated straight, with nothing sold you do not need.

faqs.question: What is the difference between bonding and grounding?
faqs.answer: Bonding ties all the metal around your pool into one network so everything sits at the same electrical level and a swimmer feels no difference in charge. Grounding gives fault current a safe path back so the breaker trips. Bonding keeps you from feeling a fault; grounding makes sure the breaker catches it. A safe pool needs both, connected correctly.

faqs.question: Why do swimmers feel tingling in the water?
faqs.answer: A tingle usually means a small amount of current is leaking onto a metal part, a rail or a light, that is not properly bonded. Because the breaker cannot sense a fault with no path back to it, it never trips, and the swimmer becomes the path instead. It is the clearest warning sign there is, and it should never be ignored.

faqs.question: How often should my pool be inspected?
faqs.answer: Once a year is the honest cadence, ideally before heater season. South Florida pools run year round, and heaters come on when the weather cools, which is when circuits work hardest. A yearly test on an older pool catches a weak or corroded bond before anyone feels it. Newer pools built to current standards need less worry.

faqs.question: Do you pull a permit for pool bonding work?
faqs.answer: When the correction calls for it, yes, and we are glad to. A permit means the building department confirms the work is right, and inspectors are thorough on pool bonding for good reason. We meet the inspector in person to prove the grounding under test. Once it passes, the safety is settled on the public record. Some minor fixes do not need a permit, and we will tell you which is which.

faqs.question: My pool looks fine. Could the bonding still be bad?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the hard part. Bonding is invisible from the deck, and a broken or corroded connection does not change how the pool looks or runs. The only way to know is to test continuity across every metal part. Electricity is something you do not see, you only feel the effect, and by the time you feel it, someone is in the water.

Any larger correction is quoted per property after we test the system, because no two older pools fail the same way. We price it once and price it right.
